s: Reddit DEF 14A filed 23 Apr 2026 (ownership as of 31 Mar 2026); RDDT close 150.31 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 629,473 shares held plus 1,633,975 exercisable options struck before the Mar 2024 IPO, valued at the RDDT close of 150.31 on 21 Aug 2026
did: Joined Reddit as chief operating officer in April 2018, when the 13-year-old site had almost no advertising business, and built the revenue organisation and self-serve ad platform that carried Reddit from under 100M dollars of annual revenue to 1.3B dollars in 2024 and through its March 2024 IPO.
why: Reddit held two decades of the highest-intent conversation on the internet and no way to sell it. Wong built ad products keyed to subreddit context, so advertisers bought declared interest communities directly instead of bidding on inferred demographics as they did on Meta.
obst: She inherited an ad surface brands actively avoided over Reddit's reputation for unmoderated content, and had to hold advertisers through the June 2023 API pricing revolt, when thousands of moderators took their subreddits private months before the IPO filing.
turn: The March 2024 IPO at 34 dollars a share, which turned six years of pre-IPO options into a marketable stake and priced the ad business she had built.

s: Figma Form 4 filed 6 Aug 2026 reporting 9,234,587 Class A shares held; FIG close 27.31 on 21 Aug 2026; age from Figma DEF 14A of 22 Apr 2026
m: 9,234,587 Class A shares per the 6 Aug 2026 Form 4 times the FIG close of 27.31 on 21 Aug 2026
did: Joined Figma as VP of engineering in April 2017, when the browser design editor was barely a year old and had no revenue, became chief technology officer in March 2022, and led engineering through the July 2025 NYSE IPO before moving off the officer roster in 2026.
why: Figma ran a full vector engine in WebGL inside a browser tab, so a design file lived at a URL rather than on one designer's laptop. That made the work reviewable by product managers and engineers, which put Figma on every team's budget rather than only the design team's.
obst: Adobe agreed to buy Figma for 20B dollars in September 2022 and abandoned the deal in December 2023 under UK and EU competition objections, leaving the engineering organisation to rebuild an independent multi-year roadmap and take the company public alone.
turn: The collapse of the Adobe acquisition in December 2023, which forced the standalone July 2025 IPO in which his equity finally became tradeable.

s: DoorDash Form 4 filed 22 Apr 2026 reporting 987,941 shares; DASH close 222.36 on 21 Aug 2026; age 43 in DoorDash S-1/A of 30 Nov 2020
m: 987,941 shares held per the 22 Apr 2026 Form 4 times the DASH close of 222.36 on 21 Aug 2026
did: Left Uber's strategic finance group in August 2018 to become DoorDash's first public-company-grade CFO, priced its December 2020 IPO at 102 dollars for a 39B dollar valuation, and became president and chief operating officer in March 2023 running marketplace, logistics and international.
why: Delivery is won on batching and drive-time density, not brand. Adarkar supplied the unit-economics discipline and the balance sheet - a 3.4B dollar IPO plus convertible notes - that let DoorDash buy suburban market density while Uber Eats and Grubhub fought over dense urban cores.
obst: He raised at a 16B dollar valuation in June 2020 while California's Proposition 22 fight threatened to reclassify every Dasher as an employee, then had to price an IPO into a market convinced that pandemic delivery demand would evaporate within a year.
turn: The December 2020 IPO, which priced above range and converted a stake he had taken as a private-company finance hire two years earlier into public equity.

s: Planet Labs DEF 14A filed 27 May 2026 (ownership as of 15 May 2026); PL close 22.29 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 12,561,847 shares held (814,949 Class A plus 11,746,898 Class B) times the PL close of 22.29 on 21 Aug 2026, excluding 4,488,288 exercisable options
did: Left NASA Ames in 2010 with Robbie Schingler and Chris Boshuizen to build Earth-imaging satellites out of consumer phone parts, shrinking a 300M dollar imaging spacecraft to a 5kg Dove; Planet now photographs the whole landmass daily and listed via SPAC in December 2021.
why: Rivals built one exquisite satellite that could see anywhere occasionally. Planet built hundreds of cheap ones that see everywhere every day, so the product is a time series rather than a photograph - and a time series sells as a subscription to agriculture, insurance and defence.
obst: Planet lost 26 satellites in the Antares launch explosion of October 2014 and eight more in the Falcon 9 failure of June 2015, and had to convince customers that a constellation model is precisely one in which individual losses do not matter.
turn: The December 2021 SPAC merger with dMY Technology IV, which put roughly 590M dollars on the balance sheet and made an eleven-year-old founder stake marketable.

s: Planet Labs DEF 14A filed 27 May 2026 (ownership as of 15 May 2026); PL close 22.29 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 12,089,980 shares held (92,911 plus 250,171 Class A and 11,746,898 Class B via the Ulysses Trust) times the PL close of 22.29 on 21 Aug 2026, excluding 1,317,379 exercisable options
did: Co-founded Planet Labs in 2010 after nine years at NASA, where he helped run the agency's small-spacecraft and open-source programmes; as chief strategy officer he built the government side of the business, including the NGA and NRO imagery contracts and the European civil-agency deals.
why: Daily global imagery only pays if a buyer with a budget is allowed to purchase it. Schingler assembled the licences, export approvals and contracting vehicles that let a commercial constellation sell to defence and intelligence customers who otherwise bought only from Maxar.
obst: US commercial remote-sensing rules were written for a handful of satellites; Planet had to get NOAA to licence hundreds at once, and to persuade intelligence buyers that unclassified medium-resolution imagery refreshed daily was worth a contract at all.
turn: The February 2017 purchase of Google's Terra Bella, which added the high-resolution SkySat fleet plus a multi-year Google imagery contract and turned Planet from a single-resolution provider into a two-tier one.

s: Fastly DEF 14A filed 22 Apr 2026 (ownership as of 15 Mar 2026); FSLY close 22.71 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 4,949,603 shares held directly and through the Bergman trusts (5,326,063 reported less 376,460 exercisable options) times the FSLY close of 22.71 on 21 Aug 2026
did: Left Wikia, where he was CTO, to found Fastly in March 2011 on the premise that a content delivery network should let a customer purge and reconfigure the edge cache in under 150 milliseconds; he was CEO until 2020, is now CTO, and took Fastly public in May 2019.
why: Akamai's edge was a static, ticket-driven configuration. Fastly made it programmable - instant purge, then Varnish VCL and later WebAssembly running at the edge - so engineers adopted it themselves instead of procurement signing a multi-year delivery contract.
obst: A single customer configuration change triggered a latent bug on 8 June 2021 that knocked out about 85 percent of Fastly's network, taking Amazon, Reddit, the New York Times and the UK government offline for roughly an hour in the most public CDN failure of the decade.
turn: The 2017 shift from selling raw bandwidth to selling edge compute and security, which is what held enterprise accounts once Cloudflare began giving the base CDN away free.

s: Asana DEF 14A filed 20 Apr 2026 (ownership as of 23 Mar 2026); ASAN close 9.50 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 12,096,018 shares held (3,773,293 Class A plus 8,898,709 Class B, less 575,984 exercisable options) times the ASAN close of 9.50 on 21 Aug 2026
did: Built Google's Drive precursor and Gmail chat as a Google product manager, prototyped the Facebook Like button at a 2007 hackathon, then left Facebook in 2008 with Dustin Moskovitz to found Asana; he was its CEO to 2010 and president to 2019 and remains a director.
why: Work-management software had always been sold to project managers as a reporting tool. Asana gave it away at the bottom to the people doing the work, so it spread through a company before procurement was ever involved - Atlassian's bottom-up motion applied to non-engineers.
obst: Asana direct-listed in September 2020 with no capital raised and no underwriter support, then fell from over 140 dollars in November 2021 to under 10 dollars, with Moskovitz personally buying stock and lending the company money to fund it through the collapse.
turn: The September 2020 direct listing on the NYSE, which made a twelve-year-old private founder stake tradeable without diluting it.

s: Cloudflare DEF 14A filed 9 Jun 2026 (ownership as of 30 Apr 2026); NET close 278.91 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 374,666 shares held directly and via Center Court Partners and trusts, plus 32,043 settleable RSUs, times the NET close of 278.91 on 21 Aug 2026; 225,750 exercisable options excluded because strikes are undisclosed
did: Became Cloudflare's chief financial officer in 2019 after serving as CFO of AMD through its near-death 2009-2012 restructuring and of GlobalFoundries; he priced the September 2019 NYSE IPO and has financed growth from 287M dollars of revenue to over 2B dollars.
why: Cloudflare gives away free what rivals meter and earns on the enterprise tail, which only works if somebody can fund years of negative free cash flow. Seifert priced the IPO and the 2021 and 2023 convertible notes that carried the free tier until enterprise revenue compounded past it.
obst: He arrived weeks before Cloudflare cut off 8chan in August 2019, forcing him to defend a content-neutrality position to investors mid-roadshow, and then priced the offering days after WeWork pulled its own IPO and soured the market on unprofitable listings.
turn: The September 2019 IPO at 15 dollars a share, completed in a window when almost nothing else could price, which established the currency his own package was denominated in.

s: Amplitude DEF 14A filed 24 Apr 2026 (ownership as of 15 Apr 2026); AMPL close 13.29 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 7,559,869 shares held (98,433 and 79,228 Class A plus 7,382,208 Class B in trust) times the AMPL close of 13.29 on 21 Aug 2026, before 645,482 exercisable options
did: Co-founded Sonalight, a voice-command app, with Spenser Skates out of MIT in 2012; when it stalled they found the internal dashboard built to debug it was the real product, relaunched as Amplitude in 2014, and direct-listed on Nasdaq in September 2021. He is chief technology officer.
why: Google Analytics counted pageviews for marketers. Amplitude measured behavioural cohorts for product managers and billed by monthly tracked users rather than seats, so the buyer had his own budget and the invoice grew automatically with the customer's own user growth.
obst: The pair burned two years and their seed money on Sonalight, a voice assistant almost nobody used, and had to accept that the throwaway analytics dashboard they had written to diagnose its failure was worth more than the product itself.
turn: The 2014 decision to abandon Sonalight entirely and sell the internal analytics tool instead, which produced paying customers within months.

s: Fitbit DEFM14A filed 6 Dec 2019 (ownership as of 5 Dec 2019); Google cash consideration of 7.35 dollars per share, deal closed 14 Jan 2021; age 43 in Fitbit DEF 14A of 9 Apr 2020
m: 15,148,344 shares held via the James Park Revocable Trust, the 2019 Annuity Trust and directly, times the 7.35 dollar cash merger price equals 111M dollars, before in-the-money pre-IPO options
did: Co-founded Fitbit in San Francisco in 2007 with Eric Friedman after two earlier startups, shipped the clip-on Fitbit Tracker in 2009, took the company public in June 2015 in the year's largest consumer-electronics IPO, and sold it to Google for 2.1B dollars in cash.
why: Fitbit put a MEMS accelerometer into a 99 dollar clip years before phones did the counting free, and wrapped it in a social leaderboard. The real moat was shelf space at Best Buy, Target and Walmart, which is exactly what Apple and the cheap Chinese band makers later took away.
obst: Fitbit recalled its entire Force line in 2014 after roughly a million units caused nickel rashes, then watched Apple Watch and 20 dollar Xiaomi bands cut the share price from 47 dollars in 2015 to under 3 dollars by 2019 - the level at which the Google sale was negotiated.
turn: The June 2015 IPO at 20 dollars a share, which converted a hardware founder's equity into a public stake at the very top of the wearables cycle.

s: Zendesk DEFM14A filed 20 Jul 2022 (ownership as of 19 Jul 2022); 77.50 dollar cash merger price, deal closed 22 Nov 2022; age 51 in Zendesk DEF 14A of 11 Jul 2022
m: 853,913 shares plus 1,593,272 exercisable options (1,096,886 struck at 9.52 dollars, 232,900 at 24.77) taken at the 77.50 dollar cash price gives about 153M dollars, on top of 57.3M dollars of option exercises disclosed for fiscal 2021
did: Founded Zendesk in a Copenhagen loft in 2007 with Alexander Aghassipour and Morten Primdahl, moved it to San Francisco in 2009, listed it on the NYSE in 2014, and sold it to Hellman and Friedman and Permira for 10.2B dollars cash in November 2022.
why: Help-desk software in 2007 meant a six-figure Siebel or Kayako installation. Zendesk sold browser-based ticketing at 9 dollars per agent per month on a credit card, so a support manager bought it without IT approval and the seat count grew as the customer hired.
obst: Zendesk shareholders voted down the board's own 4.1B dollar Momentive acquisition in February 2022, Jana Partners forced a strategic review, and a first take-private attempt collapsed in June 2022 before the company sold well below its 2021 peak valuation.
turn: The 2009 relocation from Copenhagen to San Francisco on Charles River Ventures seed money, which put the company inside the US software buyer base it needed to sell to.

s: Affirm DEF 14A filed 24 Oct 2025 (ownership as of 30 Sep 2025); AFRM close 75.05 on 21 Aug 2026; age 47 in Affirm S-1/A of 11 Jan 2021
m: 1,939,614 shares held (1,064,349 Class A including 868,114 in the Michalek 2007 Trust, plus 875,265 Class B) times the AFRM close of 75.05 on 21 Aug 2026, before 1,626,336 exercisable options
did: Joined Affirm in 2014 as an early engineering leader and is now president of technology, owning the underwriting, servicing and merchant-integration stack behind its point-of-sale instalment loans; he had previously led engineering at Google and at Max Levchin's Slide.
why: Buy-now-pay-later is a credit-underwriting business wearing a checkout button. Affirm scores each individual transaction inside the merchant's checkout in under a second on its own risk models rather than a FICO cutoff, which is why it can price 0 percent APR offers card issuers cannot.
obst: Affirm fell from 168 dollars in November 2021 to under 10 dollars in December 2022 as rates and its own funding costs rose, and the collapse of Peloton - once roughly 30 percent of revenue - forced the platform to be rebuilt around Amazon and Shopify instead.
turn: The 2020 Shopify partnership that made Affirm the default instalment option for Shopify merchants, replacing a single-customer concentration risk with distribution across hundreds of thousands of stores.
